short: Run, search and schedule Claude Code and Codex agents from tmux
long:
Komrad runs coding agents in tmux panes and keeps track of them.

There are two processes. `komrad serve` is the long-lived server that owns the
database, answers the API and the MCP endpoint, and watches every pane. The panel
is a client of it, which is why it can be closed and reopened without stopping
anything. Every other command here is a client of the same service.

`komrad open` brings the panel up in this terminal, and the other commands are
for the times something has to be done by hand: check the machine, start or stop
the server, or call an endpoint from a script.

long:
Attach the running panel in this terminal.

same panel. Detaching gives this terminal back and leaves everything running.

It attaches a panel that is already up and refuses when there is none, since
starting one is what `komrad open` is for.

Serve the forge proxy and the control plane's endpoints.

The forge proxy listens on control_plane.forge_proxy_addr for the engines control_plane.engines

short: Check that this machine has everything komrad needs
long:
Check that this machine has everything komrad needs, one line per dependency.

It checks tmux and its version, the shell tmux starts panes with, whether the
config file parses and names a harness that exists, the hooks and worktrees
directories and whether any worktree there is left without an agent, the database
and whether its schema is current, the read-only login the MCP query tools connect
as, the server on its address, and the CLI binary behind each harness and its
version. It repairs nothing, since a command that changed what it was describing
could not be trusted to say what is wrong.

It also reports what a bug report needs: the build of this binary, the operating
system with its release and architecture, and the terminal the panel is drawn in,
which inside tmux is asked of tmux, since tmux names itself to what it runs.

It also asks the terminal what it can draw. Every glyph the agents list uses is
written out and the cursor position queried, so what comes back is how far the
cursor moved rather than how wide the ink was. Inside tmux that answer comes
from tmux's own grid rather than from the terminal underneath it. Bold and
italic are read out of the terminfo entry of the terminal tmux paints to, and
colour depth out of the entry this process emits for, which is what an entry
claims rather than what a terminal does. Nothing is asked of a terminal that is
not there, and whether the font has a glyph at all is not tested.

Pointed at an engine with --engine, the checks about this machine run here and the
ones about the engine are asked of its server, which makes them on its own
machine; they are printed under an "on the engine" heading, and marked not checked
when the server cannot be reached.

The exit status is non-zero when any check failed, so it can gate a script, and
--json prints the report rather than the summary. Run this first when the panel is
doing something that makes no sense.

short: Create an engine's identity and logins, or reset their password
long:
Create an engine's identity and logins, or reset their password.

An engine is one komrad server and what it owns. Everything it writes belongs to it, and
Postgres keeps every other engine's rows out of its reach, because it connects as a login
of its own that the database maps to its identity. This creates that identity if no engine
has the name yet, a login for it and a read-only login for its MCP query tools, and the
schema its job queue lives in, connecting as owner_database_url.

Both logins take the password in KOMRAD_ENGINE_PASSWORD, or a fresh one when that is unset,
and running it again resets them to it. It prints the database_url the engine connects with.
Naming an engine that already exists, such as the default one every row written before
engines had logins belongs to, hands it new logins and keeps its rows.

short: Connect a forge with a token read from stdin, or as the engine's GitHub App
long:
Connect a forge with a token read from stdin, or as the engine's GitHub App.

With --method token, the default, the token is read from standard input, or from
the file --token-file names. It is never taken as an argument, since arguments are
visible to every process on the machine. Pipe it in:

    gh auth token | komrad forge connect github.com
    op read op://vault/github/token | komrad forge connect github.com
    komrad forge connect gitlab.com --token-file ~/.config/gitlab-token
    komrad forge connect gitlab.example.com --kind gitlab --token-file ~/.config/gitlab-token

A GitLab token is a personal access token with the api scope. A remote on an SSH
host of its own, such as ssh.gitlab.example.com, reaches the connection for its web
host once [git] ssh_hosts in the config names the pair.

With --method github-app nothing is read. The server mints a token from the App
named under [github_app] in its own config, checks the installation reaches at
least one repository, and records the App's own name as the login. That is the
engine's path, where nobody is there to paste a token and the App's key is already
on the machine: komrad forge connect github.com --method github-app --engine remote.

With --method rotating-token the token is read as for token, and the host has to
run GitLab. The token needs the api scope. The server rotates it at once and keeps
only the new one, then rotates it again each day before it expires, so the token
you pasted stops working as soon as the connection is made.

The server asks the forge who the credential belongs to before storing anything,
so a token that is wrong or expired is refused here rather than found out later.
That proves the token is real, not that it can read your repositories: a token with
no permissions answers the same question, and shows up later as a repository the
forge says it cannot find. github.com and gitlab.com say which forge they run; any
other host needs --kind, and --api-url when the API is not at https://<host>/api/v3
for GitHub or /api/v4 for GitLab. The address has to be https.

flags.usage: which forge the host runs, github or gitlab, when the host does not say

flags.name: method
flags.usage: how the credential comes: token or rotating-token from stdin, or github-app from the App in the server's config

flags.name: token-file
flags.usage: read the token from this file instead of stdin

short: Reach GitHub as the engine's own App, or through a control plane
long:
Reach GitHub as the engine's own App, or through a control plane.

An engine runs agents that write code, so it has to push. Giving it a personal
access token would leave a secret on the machine that works forever.

Instead komrad holds a GitHub App's private key and signs a short assertion with it.
GitHub returns a token that stops working after an hour and only reaches the
repositories the App was installed on.

Set the App id, the installation id and the path to the key under `[github_app]`.

An engine behind a control plane holds no App. Its person runs authorize once, and the
forge proxy adds their GitHub login to the engine's GitHub requests.

long:
Answer git when it asks for a password.

Git runs this and describes what it wants to reach. This answers only for https to
github.com. Anything else gets no answer, so git falls back to whatever else the
account has configured.

Nothing is stored. The token is made when git asks and stops working within the hour.

Set it up with:

Run this to check the App is set up. A token starting ghs_ means the key, the App id

This asks the engine which provider that is, opens the provider's sign-in page in your browser,

short: Apply any pending database migrations
long:
Apply any pending database migrations, connecting as the login that owns the schema.

The server never migrates: an engine connects as a login that cannot change the schema,
and it refuses to start against a database missing migrations its build carries. So
every upgrade runs this first, with owner_database_url (or KOMRAD_OWNER_DATABASE_URL)
naming the owner, which falls back to database_url on a database no engine has joined.

While owner_database_url names the embedded Postgres, this creates it when there is none
and starts it when it is down.

It refuses while another komrad is connected and the build holds migrations the database
has not seen, since a change it makes could break them. It is safe to run against a
database that is already current; it says so and exits zero.

short: Open the panel in this terminal, creating or attaching its persistent session
long:
Open the panel in this terminal.

It creates the manager session if it is not there and attaches either way, so the
panel keeps its place between opens rather than starting over. The manager session
lives on komrad's own tmux server, so it does not show up in `tmux ls`.

It opens this machine's panel, or the engine --engine names.

The terminal becomes the tmux client, so a detach returns to the shell. Run from
inside tmux it nests the panel in the current pane.

With --detach it creates the session and returns, which is what a script wants when
it needs somewhere for agents to be put back into.

With --headless it creates that session holding nothing but a placeholder, for an
engine whose panel runs on somebody else's machine and which would otherwise swap
an agent's pane into a panel nobody is looking at.

long:
List a repository's pull requests through the forge its host is connected to.

Give a remote as git spells it. With a branch, every pull request opened from it is
listed whatever its state; without one, the repository's open pull requests are
listed.

    komrad pr list git@github.com:harrisoncramer/komrad.git

The forge hands them over a hundred at a time and this follows every page, so the
list is whole; to read one page at a time, call the endpoint through komrad rpc
with a limit and the cursor it answers.

A repository the credential cannot see answers not found, which is how a token
without access to a private repository shows up.

short: Call the server's endpoints, one subcommand per RPC
long:
Call the server's endpoints from a script.

Every subcommand here is one RPC, named as the MCP tool surface names it, so a
script and a model ask for the same operation by the same name. Request fields are
flags, and the response is the API's own JSON on stdout.

short: Run the komrad server in the foreground
long:
Run the komrad server in the foreground.

It opens the database, mounts the Connect handlers and the MCP endpoint on one
address, runs the loops that read each pane's state and sync transcripts, and fires
schedules. The panel and the rest of these commands are clients of it, so
nothing works without it.

While connection.database_url names the embedded Postgres, it starts the
embedded Postgres first and starts it again whenever it exits.

`komrad start` spawns this detached with its output going to the log file, which is
how it usually runs. Run it here to watch that output directly. It stops on an
interrupt, or when `komrad stop` asks it to.

flags.usage: listen address, defaulting to KOMRAD_ADDR

short: Set this machine up for komrad, asking for whatever is missing
long:
Set this machine up for komrad, asking for whatever is missing.

Each step asks the doctor whether its part of the machine is ready, and only when it is not
does it ask a question and change something, then asks the doctor again. Nothing records
which steps ran, so running it again after stopping part way finds the finished steps
already done. It ends on the doctor's full report.

Setup writes the config file only when there is none, from a config template filled with
your answers. It never changes a config file that already exists: a step that would stops and
names the setting to change there.

With --no-input, or when stdin is not a terminal, nothing is asked: a step that needs an
answer takes it from a flag, and names the flag when none was given.

The database step runs while database_url is left empty. It creates the embedded Postgres
under the state directory without asking, migrates it, and makes an engine named default,
writing no connection settings. With --no-embedded-postgres it takes the url of a login that
owns a Postgres you already run instead, from --owner-database-url or by asking, and writes
the [connection] settings.

The forge step connects github.com or gitlab.com with a pasted token once the engine is
running, and skips until then. Unattended it skips, and komrad forge connect connects any
forge after setup.

flags.name: no-input
flags.usage: ask nothing, taking every answer from a flag

flags.name: owner-database-url
flags.usage: the url of a login that owns a Postgres you already run, when no database is set up

short: Carry an SSH connection to the engine over its api
long:
Carry an SSH connection to the engine over its api, between ssh and the engine's SSH server.

ssh runs this as the ProxyCommand of the host komrad login writes, and it reads and writes the
connection on its standard input and output. It sends the engine each fresh sign-in, and a message
every 20 seconds so a quiet connection stays open.

short: Start the server in the background if it is not already running
long:
Start the server in the background if it is not already running.

It asks the configured address who is there first. A server already answering is
left alone, whatever build it runs, so a rebuilt binary takes over only after
`komrad stop`. Otherwise `komrad serve` is spawned detached, with its output
going to the log file, and this waits for the address to answer before returning.

While connection.database_url names the embedded Postgres, this starts it first
if it is down, and has it reload its settings when it is up, even when the
server is already running. The server starts it again whenever it exits, and
`komrad stop` leaves it running.

Opening the panel does the same thing on its own, so this is for scripts and for
bringing the server up without a panel.

short: Ask the running server to stop, and wait until it is gone
long:
Ask the running server to stop, and wait until it is gone.

This asks rather than signals, so the server can finish the launch it is in the
middle of and say when it is done. It returns once the process has actually gone,
not when the address stops answering, which happens well before the shutdown is
finished. Nothing serving at the address is not an error.

Agents keep running: they are tmux panes, not children of this process. They are
picked back up when the server returns.

short: Attach to an agent's terminal on the engine
long:
Attach to an agent's terminal on the engine.

The terminal is carried to this one over the engine's api, so it works the same
whether the engine is this machine or another one. AGENT is the agent's id, and
the agent has to be live and hold a pane. Attaching detaches any other terminal
attached to the same agent. A dropped connection is dialled again, and since
tmux keeps the session nothing is lost. Opened before this machine signs in to
an engine at its url, it says so and attaches once komrad login runs.

long:

second line is not the first, restart the server.

short: Run the stand-in visual mode selects in
long:
Run the stand-in visual mode selects in.

Visual mode draws the sidebar as tiles on a private tmux server, one for each of
its blocks, with only the block that has the keys in copy-mode, so a selection
stops at that block's edge. This command builds that server from file, swaps a
client of it into the sidebar's place, and gives the sidebar back once copy-mode
ends. Nothing here is meant to be run by hand.
